record.paper_title: An unsolved problem on the powers of 3/2
record.original_question: Does there exist a positive real number alpha such that, for every integer n greater than or equal to 0, if alpha times (3/2)^n is written as g_n + r_n with g_n the greatest integer not greater than alpha times (3/2)^n and r_n its fractional part, then 0 <= r_n < 1/2? Equivalently, do any Z-numbers exist for the base 3/2 and the half-interval [0, 1/2)?

evidence.quote: We say that alpha is a Z-number if 0 <= r_n < 1/2 for all suffixes n >= 0.
Several years ago, a Japanese colleague proposed to me the problem whether such Z-numbers do in fact exist.

artifact.self_contained_problem: For a positive real number $\alpha$ and a non-negative integer $n$, write $\alpha\,(3/2)^n = g_n + r_n$, where $g_n = \lfloor \alpha\,(3/2)^n \rfloor$ is the greatest integer not exceeding $\alpha\,(3/2)^n$ and $r_n = \{\alpha\,(3/2)^n\} \in [0,1)$ is its fractional part. Call $\alpha$ a $Z$-number if $0 \le r_n < 1/2$ for every integer $n \ge 0$. Does there exist any $Z$-number, i.e., does there exist a positive real $\alpha$ such that the fractional part of $\alpha\,(3/2)^n$ lies in $[0,1/2)$ for all $n \ge 0$?
artifact.status_search_result: Mahler's 3/2 problem on the existence of Z-numbers remains open. Mahler (1968) conjectured no Z-numbers exist. Partial results exist (e.g., Flatto–Lagarias–Pollington bounds on the discrepancy function, and a 2024 preprint resolving a restricted integer version), but the general existence question is unresolved.

status_evidence.snippet: Mahler conjectured no Z-numbers exist; the problem remains open.
status_evidence.claim: The existence of Z-numbers is an open problem.

status_evidence.title: Mahler's 3/2 problem in Z+
status_evidence.snippet: Recent (2024) work treats a restricted version of the problem in the positive integers.
